blocks.text: A pick-and-place head must park a 0.5 mm component within 0.02 mm, and the controller must know the motor's speed to hold a constant belt feed. Both facts come from a small disc of slots on the motor shaft: an incremental encoder turns rotation into pulses that a microcontroller can count.

blocks.markdown: A **position or speed sensor** converts shaft angle or motion into an electrical signal. Simple choices include a **potentiometer** (a resistive divider whose wiper voltage is proportional to angle: cheap, analogue, limited travel) and an **incremental optical encoder**, which has a disc with a fixed number of equally spaced slots in front of a light source and detector. Each slot passing produces one pulse, so counting pulses gives angle and counting pulses per second gives speed.

blocks.title: Incremental encoder resolution
blocks.text: An encoder with $N$ pulses per revolution (PPR) on one channel has angular resolution $\Delta\theta=360^\circ/N$ per pulse. Two channels, A and B, are offset by a quarter of a pitch (quadrature), so a decoder can count all four edges per slot: counts per revolution $=4N$ and $\Delta\theta=360^\circ/(4N)$. The order of the edges (A leads B or B leads A) gives the direction of rotation.

blocks.caption: Position from count n, and shaft speed from the pulse frequency f_A of channel A (N = pulses per revolution)

blocks.title: Resolution and position
blocks.prompt: A 1024 PPR encoder is decoded in x4 quadrature mode. Find its angular resolution, and the shaft angle after a net count of 3000.
blocks.answer: Resolution 0.0879 degrees per count; a net count of 3000 corresponds to 263.7 degrees from the start.

blocks.title: Speed from pulse frequency
blocks.prompt: The same 1024 PPR encoder produces 25.6 kHz on channel A. What is the shaft speed in rev/s, rpm and rad/s?

steps.text: Pulses per second divided by pulses per revolution.

blocks.answer: 25 rev/s = 1500 rpm = 157 rad/s. At low speed it is better to measure the time between pulses; at high speed, count pulses in a fixed gate time.

blocks.markdown: **Signal conditioning for an ADC.** Many sensors (strain bridges, thermocouples, current shunts) give millivolt-level outputs, but an ADC input spans volts. An op-amp **amplifier** scales the sensor range to fill the ADC range, which makes best use of its resolution; the gain is $G=V_{ADC,max}/V_{sensor,max}$. A **low-pass filter** placed before the ADC removes noise above the signal band and prevents aliasing: its cut-off should be well below half the sampling rate, but above the highest signal frequency of interest.

blocks.caption: Gain to match sensor and ADC full scale, non-inverting gain and first-order RC filter cut-off

blocks.title: Conditioning a 0 to 20 mV sensor
blocks.prompt: A sensor outputs 0 to 20 mV. The 10-bit ADC spans 0 to 3.3 V. Choose a non-inverting gain and resistors, leaving some headroom. Then choose an RC low-pass to suppress 1 kHz noise while passing signals below 50 Hz.

steps.text: Choose $G=150$ (about 91 % of full scale), with $R_g=1$ k$\Omega$.
Filter cut-off: choose $f_c=100$ Hz. With $C=100$ nF, find $R$.

blocks.answer: Non-inverting gain of 151 (R_g = 1 k, R_f = 150 k) maps 20 mV to 3.02 V. An RC with 16 kohm and 100 nF has f_c = 99.5 Hz, which attenuates 1 kHz noise by about 10 times.

rows: Needs a reference (homing); loses position if counts are missed
blocks.caption: Position and speed sensor options

items: Higher PPR or x4 decoding gives finer angular and linear resolution.
Speed is the rate of count change: $f_A/N$ in rev/s.
Match amplifier gain to the ADC full scale, leaving a margin of 5 to 10 %.
Set the filter cut-off below half the sampling rate to avoid aliasing.

blocks.title: Resolution is not accuracy
blocks.text: An encoder's counts per revolution fix the smallest angular step, but the disc's slot-position error, mechanical backlash and mounting eccentricity limit true accuracy.

points: Incremental encoder: $\Delta\theta=360^\circ/N$ per pulse, or $360^\circ/4N$ with quadrature decoding.
Condition a low-level sensor with gain $G=V_{ADC,fs}/V_{sensor,fs}$ and an RC low-pass with $f_c=1/2\pi RC$ before the ADC.

questions.stem: A 600 PPR incremental encoder is read with only one channel and one edge counted per slot. What is the angular resolution?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: 0.15 degrees is 360/(4 x 600), the quadrature value.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this is 360/150, a misread PPR.

questions.explanation: With one count per slot the resolution is $360^\circ/N=360/600=0.6^\circ$. Quadrature decoding would improve this by a factor of four.

questions.stem: A 500 PPR encoder is decoded in x4 quadrature mode. What is the angular resolution?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: 0.72 degrees is the single-edge resolution 360/500.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: 0.045 degrees applies a further factor of 4.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this multiplies by 2 instead of dividing by 4.

questions.explanation: There are $4\times500=2000$ counts per revolution, so $\Delta\theta=360/2000=0.18^\circ$.

questions.stem: Why is a low-pass filter placed in front of an ADC input?

options.text: To remove noise above the signal band and prevent aliasing
To convert the signal to digital

questions.correctOptionText: To remove noise above the signal band and prevent aliasing

distractorRationale.a: Correct: components above half the sampling rate would fold into the band.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: resolution depends on bit depth and reference.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: a passive filter does not amplify.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: conversion is the ADC's job.

questions.explanation: Frequencies above half the sampling rate fold back into the measured band as false low-frequency signals. A filter placed before the ADC attenuates them first.

questions.stem: A 360 PPR encoder gives 3.0 kHz on channel A. What is the shaft speed?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this forgets to convert rev/s to rpm.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this multiplies pulses by PPR.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this divides by the x4 factor, which applies to counting, not to the channel A frequency.

questions.explanation: Revolutions per second are pulses per second divided by pulses per revolution: $3000/360=8.33$ rev/s. Multiply by 60 for 500 rpm.

questions.stem: A sensor gives 0 to 50 mV and must fill a 0 to 5.0 V ADC range exactly. Which non-inverting amplifier is correct?

options.text: R_f = 100 k$\Omega$ inverting with R_in = 1 k$\Omega$

distractorRationale.a: Correct: gain 1 + 99 = 100, so 50 mV gives 5.0 V.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: gain 101 gives 5.05 V, which exceeds the ADC range.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the inverting circuit would give a negative output (-5 V), outside the unipolar ADC range.

questions.explanation: The required gain is $5.0/0.050=100$. For a non-inverting stage $G=1+R_f/R_g$, so $R_f/R_g=99$, i.e. 99 k$\Omega$ with 1 k$\Omega$.

questions.stem: A lead screw has a pitch of 5.0 mm per revolution and is driven directly by a 2000 PPR encoder shaft decoded in x4 mode. What linear resolution is obtained, in micrometres?
questions.explanation: Counts per revolution are $4\times2000=8000$. One count moves the nut $5.0\ \mathrm{mm}/8000=0.625\ \mu$m.

questions.stem: A 2048 PPR encoder is decoded in x4 mode and 2400 counts are accumulated in a gate time of 50 ms. What is the shaft speed in rpm?
questions.explanation: Counts per revolution are $4\times2048=8192$, so 2400 counts is $2400/8192=0.2930$ rev. In 0.050 s this is 5.859 rev/s, which is $5.859\times60=351.6$ rpm.

questions.stem: A sensor has a full-scale output of 12 mV. The ADC range is 0 to 3.3 V and the design must use 90 % of full scale at the maximum sensor output to leave headroom. What amplifier gain is required?
questions.explanation: The target maximum is $0.90\times3.3=2.97$ V. The gain is $2.97/0.012=247.5$. For a non-inverting stage, $R_f/R_g=246.5$.

questions.stem: Explain how an incremental encoder with channels A and B determines position, direction and speed. Why does quadrature decoding improve resolution?
markingGuide: Each slot gives pulses; counting pulses gives angle = count x 360/(counts per rev)
A and B are offset by a quarter period (90 degrees electrical)
Which channel leads determines the direction of rotation
Counting all four edges per slot gives 4N counts per revolution, a 4x finer resolution
Speed from pulse frequency f_A/N or count change per gate time
questions.explanation: Counting pulses from the slotted disc gives the angle moved. Channels A and B are a quarter-period apart, so which one leads indicates the direction, and counting both edges of both channels gives $4N$ counts per revolution, four times the resolution of counting one channel. Speed follows from the pulse rate, $f_A/N$ revolutions per second.

questions.stem: A strain-gauge bridge outputs 0 to 25 mV. It is to be sampled at 1 kHz by a 12-bit ADC (0 to 3.3 V). Specify a suitable amplifier gain, a filter cut-off frequency, and state the sensor-referred voltage resolution. Justify your choices.
markingGuide: Maximum gain 3.3/0.025 = 132; chooses about 120 (headroom), giving about 3.0 V full scale
Nyquist: sampling at 1 kHz requires signals below 500 Hz; filter cut-off chosen well below, e.g. 100 to 200 Hz
Filter removes noise (mains hum, motor noise) above the signal band to prevent aliasing
questions.explanation: The largest gain that avoids clipping is $3.3/0.025=132$; a gain near 120 gives a 3.0 V full scale and some headroom. The ADC step is $3.3/4096=0.806$ mV, which referred to the sensor is $0.806/120\approx6.7\ \mu$V. With $f_s=1$ kHz, only signals below 500 Hz can be represented, so an anti-alias low-pass with $f_c$ of about 100 to 200 Hz removes noise and prevents aliasing.
